blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Choosing the right test means matching step 3 to five features of the study: the type of outcome, what is being compared (one group, two groups, more than two, or an association between two variables), whether observations are independent, paired/matched or clustered, whether the distributional assumptions of a parametric test hold, and the study design that produced the data.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Recall §1.5: the design decides which measures the data can give (prevalence from a cross-sectional survey, risk and rate from a cohort, the odds ratio of exposure from a case-control study). The outcome type decides the family of methods. The pairing or clustering decides the version within the family. Answer five questions in order:

  1. What type is the outcome: quantitative (roughly normal, or skewed), ordinal, binary, categorical, a count or rate, or a time to an event (recall §1.1.2)?
  2. What is compared: one group with a fixed value, two groups, more than two groups, or two variables measured on the same people?
  3. Are the observations independent, paired or matched (the same person twice, or matched case–control pairs), or clustered (children within villages, repeated visits)?
  4. For a quantitative outcome, are the parametric assumptions reasonable (recall the Central Limit Theorem, §6.6), or is a rank-based method safer?
  5. Which design produced the data, and therefore which effect measure is valid?

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Mean birthweight of babies of smokers and non-smokers, birthweight roughly normal: quantitative outcome, two independent groups, parametric assumptions reasonable → the independent-samples t-test (§9.2.2). If birthweight were heavily skewed with outliers → the Mann-Whitney U test (§10.2, a test on ranks) instead, or a transformation (§9.4). If the same data came from a cluster survey of 30 villages → the same comparison, but with an SE corrected for clustering (§6.2.6, §15.2).

The tables below are the map of the rest of the book. The tests and models in them are defined in the sections cited; for now read each name as a label. The last column of each table gives the regression model that does the same job while adjusting for other variables.

points.html: The design comes first. A case-control study gives the odds ratio of exposure, not a risk ratio (recall §1.5), whatever test is run on it.
Paired and clustered data break the independence assumption of the ordinary tests. Ignoring pairing usually wastes power; ignoring clustering gives SEs and p-values that are too small.

“Non-normal data, so use a non-parametric test” is too simple. With large samples the t-test is robust through the Central Limit Theorem (recall §6.6), and the choice depends also on whether the mean or the median answers the question. §10.1 (when to use non-parametric tests) sets out the choice.
A correctly computed test on the wrong design is still wrong. Choosing the method to fit the design and outcome matters as much as the arithmetic.

questions.prompt: Name the five questions you ask to choose a statistical test, and say why the design question comes first.
questions.answer: 1. Type of outcome (quantitative normal or skewed, ordinal, binary, categorical, count/rate, time to event). (2) What is compared (one group vs a value, two groups, more than two, association of two variables). (3) Independent, paired/matched, or clustered observations. (4) For quantitative outcomes, whether parametric assumptions are reasonable. (5) The study design. The design comes first because it fixes which effect measures are valid: a case-control study, for example, can give only the odds ratio of exposure, never prevalence or risk (§1.5). No choice of test can recover a measure the design cannot supply.

questions.prompt: Using Tables 8.1–8.4, choose the test and the adjusting model for: (a) haemoglobin before and after iron–folic acid in the same 12 women, with skewed differences; (b) a case-control study of neonatal sepsis with each case matched to a neighbourhood control, exposure “home delivery”; (c) full-immunisation coverage compared between urban and rural children in a 30-cluster survey.
questions.answer:
1. Quantitative, two paired measurements, skewed differences: the sign test (§10.1.1). The Wilcoxon signed-rank test (§10.3) needs roughly symmetric differences, so it fits only if the skew is mild. No regression is needed for a single before–after comparison; to adjust, model the differences (linear regression after transformation, §9.4) or use a mixed model (§15.2.4).
  2. Binary exposure, matched case-control pairs: matched-pair odds ratio b/c and McNemar’s test (§10.8); adjusting model: conditional logistic regression (§13.2.9).
  3. Binary outcome, two groups, clustered sample: difference or ratio of proportions (§10.6.4) with an SE corrected for clustering by the design effect (§6.2.6) or a survey analysis (§15.2.6); adjusting model: logistic regression with GEE or survey weights and PSUs (§15.2.5, §15.2.6). An ordinary chi-square would give a p-value that is too small.

questions.prompt: In a cohort, 30 of 150 exposed and 15 of 150 unexposed people develop the outcome. Following the seven steps of §8.7, compute the risk difference, the pooled SE under H₀, z and the two-sided p, and the 95% CI of the difference (unpooled SE). State the conclusion.
questions.answer:
1. H₀: risk exposed = risk unexposed; H₁: they differ (two-tailed).
  2. α = 0.05.
  3. Binary outcome, two independent groups → two-proportion z-test (or chi-square). Pooled risk 45/300 = 0.15; under H₀ each group expects 150 × 0.15 = 22.5 events and 127.5 non-events, ample for the normal approximation (§5.7.2.2.4).
  4. Risks 30/150 = 0.20 and 15/150 = 0.10; risk difference = 0.10. SE₀ = √[0.15 × 0.85 × (1/150 + 1/150)] = √(0.1275 × 0.01333) = √0.0017 = 0.0412. z = 0.10/0.0412 = 2.43.
  5. Two-sided p = 2 × [1 − Φ(2.43)] = 0.015.
  6. 0.015 < 0.05: reject H₀.
  7. Unpooled SE = √(0.20 × 0.80/150 + 0.10 × 0.90/150) = √(0.001067 + 0.000600) = 0.0408. 95% CI = 0.10 ± 1.96 × 0.0408 = 0.10 ± 0.080 = 0.020 to 0.180. Conclusion: the risk was 10 percentage points higher in the exposed (20% vs 10%; 95% CI 2.0 to 18.0 points; p = 0.015). The interval is wide: the data are compatible with a small (2 points) or a large (18 points) excess risk. It is an association; confounding has not been addressed.
